## Introduction
Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) is an autonomic nervous system disorder characterized by an excessive heart rate increase of at least 30 beats per minute (or 40 beats per minute in adolescents) within 10 minutes of standing, in the absence of orthostatic hypotension, often accompanied by symptoms such as lightheadedness, fatigue, and palpitations.1,2 Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS) is a group of connective tissue disorders that result in hypermobile joints, skin hyperextensibility, and tissue fragility.3 Both conditions are increasingly recognized to occur concurrently with mast cell activation disorders (MCADs), which represent a spectrum of conditions involving inappropriate mast cell activation and mediator release. MCADs include mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS; most frequently associated condition), idiopathic, monoclonal, and secondary types, including systemic mastocytosis.4 Another condition, hereditary alpha tryptasemia (HAT), has been associated with more severe symptoms in patients with IgE and non–IgE-mediated mast cell activation, especially in patients with venom allergy, and possibly in mastocytosis.5
Although anecdotal and clinical observations suggest a potential relationship among POTS, EDS, and MCADs/HAT, the evidence supporting this association remains unclear. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of MCADs and HAT in patients diagnosed with having EDS and/or POTS.

## Results
Our search identified a total of 198 records after duplicate removal, and we added 2 external studies identified through citation searching.11,12 We excluded 107 studies based on the title or abstract. We were unable to retrieve 1 record and reviewed a total of 92 full texts. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic review evaluating the potential association between POTS and EDS with MCADs. We identified no adequate studies demonstrating an association between these conditions that used our prespecified diagnostic criteria.

# Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome and Hypermobility: Understanding the Whole-Body Pattern
## Bringing the Whole Pattern Together
Joint instability can increase muscle guarding. Muscle guarding can increase pain and energy demand. Poor sleep can increase pain sensitivity and mast-cell reactivity. Dysautonomia can increase adrenaline, dizziness, and fatigue. Gastrointestinal dysfunction can reduce nutrient absorption. Histamine can affect sleep, heart rate, digestion, and nervous-system activation. Genetic variants shape how efficiently each pathway responds.
This interconnected physiology is why supporting one symptom in isolation often produces limited results. Someone with POTS, low ferritin, DAO-related histamine pressure, and slower COMT needs a different plan from someone whose primary concern is tendon injury with otherwise stable digestion and circulation. Gene variants are indicators of nutritional load and physiological tendency, not diagnoses or fixed outcomes.
Your symptoms carry information about circulation, nervous-system activity, connective-tissue demand, digestion, immune signaling, and nutrient handling. Genetics can add another layer of clarity. Laboratory testing can identify correctable deficiencies. Careful tracking can reveal triggers. A physiology-first, genetics-informed approach brings these systems together and allows nutrients to be selected with intention, at a pace your body can actually use.

## Introduction
Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) is an autonomic nervous system disorder characterized by an excessive heart rate increase of at least 30 beats per minute (or 40 beats per minute in adolescents) within 10 minutes of standing, in the absence of orthostatic hypotension, often accompanied by symptoms such as lightheadedness, fatigue, and palpitations.1,2 Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS) is a group of connective tissue disorders that result in hypermobile joints, skin hyperextensibility, and tissue fragility.3 Both conditions are increasingly recognized to occur concurrently with mast cell activation disorders (MCADs), which represent a spectrum of conditions involving inappropriate mast cell activation and mediator release. MCADs include mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS; most frequently associated condition), idiopathic, monoclonal, and secondary types, including systemic mastocytosis.4 Another condition, hereditary alpha tryptasemia (HAT), has been associated with more severe symptoms in patients with IgE and non–IgE-mediated mast cell activation, especially in patients with venom allergy, and possibly in mastocytosis.5
Although anecdotal and clinical observations suggest a potential relationship among POTS, EDS, and MCADs/HAT, the evidence supporting this association remains unclear. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of MCADs and HAT in patients diagnosed with having EDS and/or POTS.

Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) is an autonomic nervous system disorder characterized by an excessive heart rate increase of at least 30 beats per minute (or 40 beats per minute in adolescents) within 10 minutes of standing, in the absence of orthostatic hypotension, often accompanied by symptoms such as lightheadedness, fatigue, and palpitations.1,2 Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS) is a group of connective tissue disorders that result in hypermobile joints, skin hyperextensibility, and tissue fragility.3 Both conditions are increasingly recognized to occur concurrently with mast cell activation disorders (MCADs), which represent a spectrum of conditions involving inappropriate mast cell activation and mediator release. MCADs include mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS; most frequently associated condition), idiopathic, monoclonal, and secondary types, including systemic mastocytosis.4 Another condition, hereditary alpha tryptasemia (HAT), has been associated with more severe symptoms in patients with IgE and non–IgE-mediated mast cell activation, especially in patients with venom allergy, and possibly in mastocytosis.5
Although anecdotal and clinical observations suggest a potential relationship among POTS, EDS, and MCADs/HAT, the evidence supporting this association remains unclear. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of MCADs and HAT in patients diagnosed with having EDS and/or POTS.

**By Dr. David Traster, DC, MS, DACNB**
Co-owner, _The Neurologic Wellness Institute_
Boca Raton • Chicago • Waukesha • Wood Dale www.neurologicwellnessinstitute.com
For many years, patients with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (hEDS) were often told that their symptoms existed in isolation. Joint pain was considered orthopedic. Dizziness was considered autonomic. Rashes and flushing were considered allergic. Gastrointestinal symptoms were considered functional. Fatigue was blamed on stress. Yet over time, clinicians began noticing a pattern that was difficult to ignore: many patients with hypermobility also demonstrated symptoms consistent with abnormal mast cell activity.
Today, there is growing interest in the overlap between hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and Mast Cell Activation Syndrome (MCAS). While the relationship is still being actively studied, clinical observations and emerging research suggest these conditions frequently coexist and may influence one another in meaningful ways.
Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is a hereditary connective tissue disorder characterized by joint hypermobility, tissue fragility, chronic pain, and widespread multisystem involvement. Unlike some other forms of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, the exact genetic cause of hEDS remains unclear in most cases.
Connective tissue is everywhere in the body. It supports joints, stabilizes blood vessels, forms fascia, lines the gastrointestinal tract, and plays a role in nervous system structure and signaling. When connective tissue is altered, as it is in hEDS, the effects can extend far beyond the musculoskeletal system.
Many individuals with hEDS experience:
*   Joint instability and pain

*   Chronic fatigue

*   Brain fog

*   Dizziness or POTS-like symptoms

*   Gastrointestinal dysfunction

*   Headaches

*   Flushing and skin sensitivity

*   Medication intolerance

*   Allergic-type symptoms
This broad symptom profile is one reason mast cell involvement has become an area of interest.
Mast cells are immune cells that reside primarily within connective tissue. They act as frontline responders, especially in areas exposed to the external environment such as the skin, lungs, and gastrointestinal tract.

When activated, mast cells release chemical mediators including histamine, tryptase, cytokines, leukotrienes, and prostaglandins. These substances help coordinate immune responses and inflammation. In normal physiology, this is protective. But when mast cells become dysregulated, they may release these mediators excessively or inappropriately.
In Mast Cell Activation Syndrome, this dysregulation can lead to symptoms such as:
*   Flushing

*   Itching or hives

*   Gastrointestinal distress

*   Rapid heart rate

*   Dizziness

*   Brain fog

*   Fatigue

*   Headaches

*   Sensitivity to foods, chemicals, or medications

*   Blood pressure instability
Because mast cells live inside connective tissue, researchers began questioning whether abnormalities in connective tissue could influence mast cell behavior.
One of the most consistent observations in clinical practice is that individuals with hEDS appear to have higher rates of mast-cell-related symptoms. This has led to several proposed mechanisms explaining the overlap.
Mast cells are embedded in connective tissue. In hEDS, the extracellular matrix and collagen structure are altered. This means mast cells are functioning within a different physical and biochemical environment than normal.
Some researchers propose that these structural changes may lower the activation threshold of mast cells or make them more reactive to mechanical stress. Everyday forces such as stretch, pressure, or micro-injury could potentially trigger exaggerated mast cell responses. This concept falls under mechanobiology, where physical properties of tissue influence cellular behavior.
The relationship may also be bidirectional. Mast cells release substances like histamine and proteases that can influence connective tissue integrity, vascular permeability, and inflammatory signaling.
Over time, this may contribute to:
*   Increased tissue laxity

*   Vascular instability

*   Chronic inflammation

*   Impaired tissue repair
This creates a potential feedback loop:
abnormal connective tissue influences mast cells, and activated mast cells further impact connective tissue.
Another major point of overlap is dysautonomia.
Many individuals with hEDS experience symptoms such as:
*   Orthostatic intolerance

*   POTS

*   Heart rate variability

*   Blood pressure instability

*   Heat intolerance

*   Gastrointestinal dysmotility

Mast cell mediators can directly affect vascular tone, heart rate, and nervous system signaling. Histamine, for example, can cause vasodilation, influence heart rate, and alter neural communication.
At the same time, the autonomic nervous system plays a role in regulating immune function. There is constant communication between mast cells and nerve fibers, especially sensory and autonomic nerves. This suggests that dysfunction in one system may amplify dysfunction in the other.
The gastrointestinal system is another area where this overlap becomes clear.
Patients with hEDS frequently report:
*   Bloating

*   Nausea

*   Reflux

*   Constipation or diarrhea

*   Abdominal pain

*   Food sensitivities
Mast cells are abundant in the gut and play a role in maintaining the intestinal barrier, regulating immune responses, and facilitating communication between the gut and brain.
When mast cells become overactive, they may contribute to:
*   Increased intestinal permeability

*   Visceral hypersensitivity

*   Altered motility

*   Neuroimmune signaling changes
This may help explain why gastrointestinal symptoms are so common in both hEDS and MCAS.
The current body of research shows a consistent clinical association between hEDS, MCAS, and autonomic dysfunction. Many observational studies and clinical reports describe these conditions occurring together at higher rates than expected.
However, there is still ongoing debate within the scientific community.
Key limitations include:
*   Lack of universally accepted diagnostic criteria for MCAS

*   Variability in how patients are classified

*   Limited large-scale mechanistic studies

*   Potential for symptom overlap to be misattributed
Some researchers argue that while the association appears real clinically, the underlying biological mechanisms have not yet been definitively proven.
This highlights an important concept in medicine: patterns are often recognized clinically before they are fully understood scientifically.
Emerging research is shifting toward a systems-based understanding of these conditions.
Rather than viewing connective tissue, immune function, and autonomic regulation as separate systems, newer models emphasize their integration. These systems constantly communicate through mechanical, chemical, and neural signaling pathways.
Areas of growing interest include:
*   Extracellular matrix signaling

*   Neuroimmune communication

*   Mechanobiology

*   Small fiber nerve involvement

*   Chronic inflammatory signaling

*   Connective tissue–immune interactions
This integrated perspective may better explain why patients experience such widespread and interconnected symptoms.

The overlap between hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and Mast Cell Activation Syndrome represents a complex and evolving area of medicine. While definitive answers are still emerging, the clinical patterns are difficult to ignore.
For many patients, this connection helps make sense of a constellation of symptoms that once seemed unrelated. It suggests that the body’s structural framework, immune system, and nervous system are not operating independently, but as part of a highly interconnected network.
As research continues to evolve, this relationship may offer important insights into not only hEDS and MCAS, but the broader understanding of chronic multisystem conditions and the biology that connects them.

Title: The Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome and Mast Cell Activation Syndrome Connection
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4
**By Dr. David Traster, DC, MS, DACNB**
Co-owner, _The Neurologic Wellness Institute_
Boca Raton • Chicago • Waukesha • Wood Dale www.neurologicwellnessinstitute.com
For many years, patients with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (hEDS) were often told that their symptoms existed in isolation. Joint pain was considered orthopedic. Dizziness was considered autonomic. Rashes and flushing were considered allergic. Gastrointestinal symptoms were considered functional. Fatigue was blamed on stress. Yet over time, clinicians began noticing a pattern that was difficult to ignore: many patients with hypermobility also demonstrated symptoms consistent with abnormal mast cell activity.
Today, there is growing interest in the overlap between hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and Mast Cell Activation Syndrome (MCAS). While the relationship is still being actively studied, clinical observations and emerging research suggest these conditions frequently coexist and may influence one another in meaningful ways.
Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is a hereditary connective tissue disorder characterized by joint hypermobility, tissue fragility, chronic pain, and widespread multisystem involvement. Unlike some other forms of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, the exact genetic cause of hEDS remains unclear in most cases.
Connective tissue is everywhere in the body. It supports joints, stabilizes blood vessels, forms fascia, lines the gastrointestinal tract, and plays a role in nervous system structure and signaling. When connective tissue is altered, as it is in hEDS, the effects can extend far beyond the musculoskeletal system.
Many individuals with hEDS experience:
*   Joint instability and pain

*   Chronic fatigue

*   Brain fog

*   Dizziness or POTS-like symptoms

*   Gastrointestinal dysfunction

*   Headaches

*   Flushing and skin sensitivity

*   Medication intolerance

*   Allergic-type symptoms
This broad symptom profile is one reason mast cell involvement has become an area of interest.
Mast cells are immune cells that reside primarily within connective tissue. They act as frontline responders, especially in areas exposed to the external environment such as the skin, lungs, and gastrointestinal tract.

When activated, mast cells release chemical mediators including histamine, tryptase, cytokines, leukotrienes, and prostaglandins. These substances help coordinate immune responses and inflammation. In normal physiology, this is protective. But when mast cells become dysregulated, they may release these mediators excessively or inappropriately.
In Mast Cell Activation Syndrome, this dysregulation can lead to symptoms such as:
*   Flushing

*   Itching or hives

*   Gastrointestinal distress

*   Rapid heart rate

*   Dizziness

*   Brain fog

*   Fatigue

*   Headaches

*   Sensitivity to foods, chemicals, or medications

*   Blood pressure instability
Because mast cells live inside connective tissue, researchers began questioning whether abnormalities in connective tissue could influence mast cell behavior.
One of the most consistent observations in clinical practice is that individuals with hEDS appear to have higher rates of mast-cell-related symptoms. This has led to several proposed mechanisms explaining the overlap.
Mast cells are embedded in connective tissue. In hEDS, the extracellular matrix and collagen structure are altered. This means mast cells are functioning within a different physical and biochemical environment than normal.
Some researchers propose that these structural changes may lower the activation threshold of mast cells or make them more reactive to mechanical stress. Everyday forces such as stretch, pressure, or micro-injury could potentially trigger exaggerated mast cell responses. This concept falls under mechanobiology, where physical properties of tissue influence cellular behavior.
The relationship may also be bidirectional. Mast cells release substances like histamine and proteases that can influence connective tissue integrity, vascular permeability, and inflammatory signaling.
Over time, this may contribute to:
*   Increased tissue laxity

*   Vascular instability

*   Chronic inflammation

*   Impaired tissue repair
This creates a potential feedback loop:
abnormal connective tissue influences mast cells, and activated mast cells further impact connective tissue.
Another major point of overlap is dysautonomia.
Many individuals with hEDS experience symptoms such as:
*   Orthostatic intolerance

*   POTS

*   Heart rate variability

*   Blood pressure instability

*   Heat intolerance

*   Gastrointestinal dysmotility

Mast cell mediators can directly affect vascular tone, heart rate, and nervous system signaling. Histamine, for example, can cause vasodilation, influence heart rate, and alter neural communication.
At the same time, the autonomic nervous system plays a role in regulating immune function. There is constant communication between mast cells and nerve fibers, especially sensory and autonomic nerves. This suggests that dysfunction in one system may amplify dysfunction in the other.
The gastrointestinal system is another area where this overlap becomes clear.
Patients with hEDS frequently report:
*   Bloating

*   Nausea

*   Reflux

*   Constipation or diarrhea

*   Abdominal pain

*   Food sensitivities
Mast cells are abundant in the gut and play a role in maintaining the intestinal barrier, regulating immune responses, and facilitating communication between the gut and brain.
When mast cells become overactive, they may contribute to:
*   Increased intestinal permeability

*   Visceral hypersensitivity

*   Altered motility

*   Neuroimmune signaling changes
This may help explain why gastrointestinal symptoms are so common in both hEDS and MCAS.
The current body of research shows a consistent clinical association between hEDS, MCAS, and autonomic dysfunction. Many observational studies and clinical reports describe these conditions occurring together at higher rates than expected.
However, there is still ongoing debate within the scientific community.
Key limitations include:
*   Lack of universally accepted diagnostic criteria for MCAS

*   Variability in how patients are classified

*   Limited large-scale mechanistic studies

*   Potential for symptom overlap to be misattributed
Some researchers argue that while the association appears real clinically, the underlying biological mechanisms have not yet been definitively proven.
This highlights an important concept in medicine: patterns are often recognized clinically before they are fully understood scientifically.
Emerging research is shifting toward a systems-based understanding of these conditions.
Rather than viewing connective tissue, immune function, and autonomic regulation as separate systems, newer models emphasize their integration. These systems constantly communicate through mechanical, chemical, and neural signaling pathways.
Areas of growing interest include:
*   Extracellular matrix signaling

*   Neuroimmune communication

*   Mechanobiology

*   Small fiber nerve involvement

*   Chronic inflammatory signaling

*   Connective tissue–immune interactions
This integrated perspective may better explain why patients experience such widespread and interconnected symptoms.

The overlap between hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and Mast Cell Activation Syndrome represents a complex and evolving area of medicine. While definitive answers are still emerging, the clinical patterns are difficult to ignore.
For many patients, this connection helps make sense of a constellation of symptoms that once seemed unrelated. It suggests that the body’s structural framework, immune system, and nervous system are not operating independently, but as part of a highly interconnected network.
As research continues to evolve, this relationship may offer important insights into not only hEDS and MCAS, but the broader understanding of chronic multisystem conditions and the biology that connects them.

# What is EDS?
### What causes EDS?    Each type of EDS is caused by variants in specific genes that provide the instructions for making collagens and related proteins. Some types of EDS are associated with multiple different genes. The genetic cause(s) of hEDS have not been identified.
*

# What is EDS?
### What are connective tissue and collagen?    Connective tissue is found throughout the body, where it provides support, protection, and structure to other parts of the body. Connective tissue disorders are caused by issues that prevent connective tissue from functioning properly.
Collagen is the primary component of connective tissue. There are different types of collagens with different functions. The Ehlers-Danlos syndromes are caused by changes in the genes that affect the structure and function of collagen and related connective tissue proteins.      
*

# What is EDS?
### Can EDS be inherited?    The Ehlers-Danlos syndromes can be passed on from parent to child. Each type of EDS is inherited in either a dominant or recessive inheritance pattern.
A dominant inheritance pattern means that just one copy of a genetic variant (passed down from one parent) is needed to inherit the condition. If a person has a condition with a dominant inheritance pattern, each of their children will have a 50% chance of inheriting the condition. A recessive inheritance pattern means that a person must inherit two copies of the genetic variant (one from each parent) in order to have the condition.
Although the genetic cause(s) of hEDS are not yet known, family histories suggest this condition has a dominant inheritance pattern.
A person may be the first one in their family to have a type of EDS. This is called a de novo mutation. You can read more about the inheritance of EDS here.      
*

# What is EDS?
### What are the signs and symptoms of EDS?    Each type of EDS is associated with different symptoms and characteristics. Some symptoms are common across all types of EDS, such as joint hypermobility, pain, and fatigue. Other symptoms are only observed in specific types of EDS. Even within the same type of EDS, people can experience very different symptoms from each other.
There are also many other medical conditions that are often seen in people with EDS. These include types of dysautonomia and mast cell diseases. These are often called comorbidities or comorbid conditions.      
*

# What is EDS?
### How is EDS diagnosed?    Each type of EDS has its own clinical diagnostic criteria. Clinical diagnostic criteria are a set of symptoms and characteristics observed in each condition. If a person meets the diagnostic criteria for a type of EDS, a genetic test should be done to confirm the diagnosis.
The genetic cause(s) of hEDS have not yet been identified, so there is currently no genetic test available to diagnose hEDS. The diagnosis of hEDS is given to those who meet the clinical diagnostic criteria for hEDS.
If a person has symptomatic joint hypermobility but does not meet the diagnostic criteria for any type of EDS or other condition that can cause similar symptoms, then the hypermobility spectrum disorders (HSD) should be considered. You can read more about HSD here.      
*

# What is EDS?
### How is EDS managed?    There are no disease-specific treatments for any type of EDS, so EDS is managed by addressing each person’s symptoms.The Ehlers-Danlos syndromes can cause a variety of symptoms in different areas of the body. Therefore, people with a type of EDS often require multiple providers in different specialties to manage their care. Even within the same type of EDS, two people may have very different symptoms and respond differently to different management strategies. Each person should work with their care team to develop a care plan that meets their individual needs.
*

# What is EDS?
### How were the Ehlers-Danlos syndromes named?    The **E**hlers-**D**anlos **s**yndromes (EDS) are named after two doctors, Dr. Edvard Lauritz Ehlers and Dr. Henri-Alexandre Danlos, who described the condition in the early twentieth century.
The classification of the types of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome has changed over time as these conditions were better understood. In 1986, the Berlin classification introduced 11 types of EDS, each designated by a Roman numeral. In 1998, the Villefranche classification was established based on an updated understanding of the types of EDS and their genetic causes. It included 6 types of EDS and replaced the Roman numeral system with descriptive names for each type. Major and minor criteria were also established for each type of EDS.
In 2017, The International Consortium on EDS and HSD published the 2017 international classification of the Ehlers-Danlos syndromes. This current classification includes 13 types of EDS. Each type of EDS has a descriptive name which is abbreviated using a lowercase letter to differentiate between the types of EDS. For example, hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is abbreviated to hEDS. The different types of EDS are no longer described using numbers or Roman numerals; the terms EDS type 3 and EDS type III are no longer used.
The 2017 classification also introduced the hypermobility spectrum disorders (HSD). As of 2017, joint hypermobility syndrome (JHS) and benign joint hypermobility syndrome (BJHS) are outdated terms that should no longer be used when making a diagnosis. Most people who were previously diagnosed with joint hypermobility syndrome or a similar diagnosis are now classified as having either hEDS or a type of HSD. If someone was diagnosed with hEDS before the 2017 criteria, there is no reason to seek a new diagnosis unless they decide to participate in research or need to be reassessed for some other reason.
Since the 2017 classification, researchers have identified additional genetic variants that cause symptoms similar to those seen in the Ehlers-Danlos syndromes. These variants may represent new types of EDS or may fall under one of the current types of EDS.

### How were the Ehlers-Danlos syndromes named?    The **E**hlers-**D**anlos **s**yndromes (EDS) are named after two doctors, Dr. Edvard Lauritz Ehlers and Dr. Henri-Alexandre Danlos, who described the condition in the early twentieth century.

# What is EDS?
### What are connective tissue and collagen?    Connective tissue is found throughout the body, where it provides support, protection, and structure to other parts of the body. Connective tissue disorders are caused by issues that prevent connective tissue from functioning properly.
Collagen is the primary component of connective tissue. There are different types of collagens with different functions. The Ehlers-Danlos syndromes are caused by changes in the genes that affect the structure and function of collagen and related connective tissue proteins.      
*

# What is EDS?
### Can EDS be inherited?    The Ehlers-Danlos syndromes can be passed on from parent to child. Each type of EDS is inherited in either a dominant or recessive inheritance pattern.
A dominant inheritance pattern means that just one copy of a genetic variant (passed down from one parent) is needed to inherit the condition. If a person has a condition with a dominant inheritance pattern, each of their children will have a 50% chance of inheriting the condition. A recessive inheritance pattern means that a person must inherit two copies of the genetic variant (one from each parent) in order to have the condition.
Although the genetic cause(s) of hEDS are not yet known, family histories suggest this condition has a dominant inheritance pattern.
A person may be the first one in their family to have a type of EDS. This is called a de novo mutation. You can read more about the inheritance of EDS here.      
*
texts.16:
# What is EDS?
### What are the signs and symptoms of EDS?    Each type of EDS is associated with different symptoms and characteristics. Some symptoms are common across all types of EDS, such as joint hypermobility, pain, and fatigue. Other symptoms are only observed in specific types of EDS. Even within the same type of EDS, people can experience very different symptoms from each other.
There are also many other medical conditions that are often seen in people with EDS. These include types of dysautonomia and mast cell diseases. These are often called comorbidities or comorbid conditions.      
*
texts.17:
# What is EDS?
### How is EDS diagnosed?    Each type of EDS has its own clinical diagnostic criteria. Clinical diagnostic criteria are a set of symptoms and characteristics observed in each condition. If a person meets the diagnostic criteria for a type of EDS, a genetic test should be done to confirm the diagnosis.
The genetic cause(s) of hEDS have not yet been identified, so there is currently no genetic test available to diagnose hEDS. The diagnosis of hEDS is given to those who meet the clinical diagnostic criteria for hEDS.
If a person has symptomatic joint hypermobility but does not meet the diagnostic criteria for any type of EDS or other condition that can cause similar symptoms, then the hypermobility spectrum disorders (HSD) should be considered. You can read more about HSD here.      
*
texts.18:
# What is EDS?
### How is EDS managed?    There are no disease-specific treatments for any type of EDS, so EDS is managed by addressing each person’s symptoms.The Ehlers-Danlos syndromes can cause a variety of symptoms in different areas of the body. Therefore, people with a type of EDS often require multiple providers in different specialties to manage their care. Even within the same type of EDS, two people may have very different symptoms and respond differently to different management strategies. Each person should work with their care team to develop a care plan that meets their individual needs.
*

# What is EDS?
### How were the Ehlers-Danlos syndromes named?    The **E**hlers-**D**anlos **s**yndromes (EDS) are named after two doctors, Dr. Edvard Lauritz Ehlers and Dr. Henri-Alexandre Danlos, who described the condition in the early twentieth century.
The classification of the types of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome has changed over time as these conditions were better understood. In 1986, the Berlin classification introduced 11 types of EDS, each designated by a Roman numeral. In 1998, the Villefranche classification was established based on an updated understanding of the types of EDS and their genetic causes. It included 6 types of EDS and replaced the Roman numeral system with descriptive names for each type. Major and minor criteria were also established for each type of EDS.
In 2017, The International Consortium on EDS and HSD published the 2017 international classification of the Ehlers-Danlos syndromes. This current classification includes 13 types of EDS. Each type of EDS has a descriptive name which is abbreviated using a lowercase letter to differentiate between the types of EDS. For example, hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is abbreviated to hEDS. The different types of EDS are no longer described using numbers or Roman numerals; the terms EDS type 3 and EDS type III are no longer used.
The 2017 classification also introduced the hypermobility spectrum disorders (HSD). As of 2017, joint hypermobility syndrome (JHS) and benign joint hypermobility syndrome (BJHS) are outdated terms that should no longer be used when making a diagnosis. Most people who were previously diagnosed with joint hypermobility syndrome or a similar diagnosis are now classified as having either hEDS or a type of HSD. If someone was diagnosed with hEDS before the 2017 criteria, there is no reason to seek a new diagnosis unless they decide to participate in research or need to be reassessed for some other reason.
Since the 2017 classification, researchers have identified additional genetic variants that cause symptoms similar to those seen in the Ehlers-Danlos syndromes. These variants may represent new types of EDS or may fall under one of the current types of EDS.
